doc.title: Phil Flanigan interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 15, 1998

title: Scott Hamilton's welcome in New York and Coltrane's dominance
summary: Hamilton's swing playing was embraced by veterans at Michael's Pub, leading to talk of Coltrane and academia.

story.theme_name: Playing with Coltrane and the avant-garde

blocks.x: Yeah, cracking the New York market, meeting people, getting out, playing jam sessions, hoping to play a gig and get a good recommendation?

Well that happened because of Roy Eldridge, in Scott Hamilton’s case. Scott preceded me into New York by about six months. He immediately had a gig at Michael’s Pub with Hank Jones, Milt Hinton, himself, and I can’t remember who the drummer was, it was somebody great. You know I can’t even remember, it may have been Jo Jones or somebody, or Connie Kay or one of those.

Grady, possibly Grady. I can’t remember who the drummer was, forgive me whoever it was, but so they warmed up to Scott immediately there, because he’s playing music from their era and nobody has done this, everybody is going [scats] for twenty-five years before that. You know going one-four [scats]. These are my ways of making the over- academicized music sort of to turn it into an onomatopoeia if you will. See I can do it too, academia.

Yeah, just the ridiculousness of that over studied, under feeling sort of music. So they really embraced him because they hadn’t heard anybody play a tenor saxophone without John Coltrane in mind, for like I said well probably fifteen, twenty years or better than that.
Yeah, Coltrane really like, well he predominated the scene much as Parker did I guess.

Even more so, because when Parker was alive they didn’t have all the schools that cranked out a cookie cutterized viewpoint having to do with what’s important in a various categorized box of music. Generally to academia they pick it apart and analyze it. If you do that, something with the most detail, it’s going to be the most interesting, so something like Coltrane is the most interesting. I love Coltrane myself, except for the final period, and that’s good for what it’s good for. But most people, like this kind of © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -7-

festival that we’re at now, is more traditional, and I can understand why that is. Because like language, jazz has a vocabulary and the vocabulary that’s being spoken in a traditional situation like this is the vocabulary that is the basic words of the language. Now you can get very off on a tangent and get into all sorts of technical terms and that’s what Coltrane would be doing, you know, taking the basic knowledge and taking it off and extrapolating it way out on one tangent or another, and saying, like reporting back what’s out there. And I think that’s great, I love that. I mean most of my really favorite artists are guys that have done that to some degree or other like Jimmy Rowles — stylistically way off on a tangent, musically correct but a little on the obtuse side, a little on the askew sort of thing. Getting back to my original point—
